title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted unsafe network changes versus LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload. In a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N=500 distinct synthetic intents (shared single initial candidate per intent) with generation by gpt-5-mini and adjudication by a deterministic verifier. Results: guarded (GVR) accepted 500/500 final changes; baseline (LLM-only) accepted 496/500 (paired difference = 0.008). The preregistered conditional exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant pairs (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125 computed as p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = 2*(1/16). An exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.002, 0.016] (bootstrap exploratory per preregistration and interpreted cautiously given only four discordants). Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; total model calls used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls). The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed. Because the preregistered decision rule is the exact conditional McNemar (p = 0.125), we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. We reconcile the conditional McNemar and the exploratory bootstrap CI, document verifier scope and blind spots, provide execution accounting and representative validator traces, and give explicit artifact pointers and hashes for reproducibility.

sections.introduction:
Automating operator intent→device configuration translation can materially reduce manual effort but introduces operational risk when generated CLI sequences or intermediate workflows create unsafe transient states (e.g., both ends of a link down, inadvertent VLAN moves). Recent work applies large language models (LLMs) to NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration generation, AIOps), yet hallucination and factual errors remain central deployment barriers. Tool‑augmented architectures—LLMs invoking deterministic verifiers or domain tools—are proposed to mitigate such risks, but systematic empirical comparisons with preregistered inference are limited.

This paper asks: Does a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → bounded automated repair) produce fewer accepted unsafe network changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload? We answer with a preregistered paired trial (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) executed end‑to‑end. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered N=500 paired experiment comparing GVR to a baseline LLM‑only acceptance flow (shared initial candidate per intent) with archived execution artifacts; (2) a concrete description of deterministic verifier semantics, the repair template, and provider accounting showing model‑call cost of a bounded repair policy; (3) reconciled inferential reporting that preserves the preregistered exact McNemar decision rule while also presenting a predeclared exploratory bootstrap interval and a careful caveat about small‑discordant counts; and (4) complete execution accounting, representative validator traces, and explicit reproducibility artifact hashes.
sections.related_work: Prior surveys and system papers document active interest in LLM‑assisted NetOps across intent translation, configuration generation, and AIOps; these works emphasize hallucination and factual errors as deployment barriers (surveys and system reports summarized in the evidence bundle). Methodological work on tool‑augmented LLMs and generate–validate–repair architectures stresses standardized evaluation and verifier coverage assessments. Deterministic verification tools (Batfish‑style analyzers and distributed verifiers) provide oracles for many syntactic and workflow properties but are limited by modeling abstractions (reachability, control‑plane timing). Our experiment situates itself at the intersection of these literatures by (a) using a deterministic verifier as the operational adjudicator; (b) preregistering paired confirmatory inference; and (c) archiving full artifacts for independent inspection. Representative prior works used for positioning are included in the cited_record_ids list and were verified during the autonomous literature review.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: The study preregistration (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29; preregistration SHA‑256 = aa8982a27c73e51521ac023a78adcfa358ef3978c0f9bc05213801fcbd2f1d0a) fixed the paired confirmatory design, the estimand, sampling plan, stopping rule, and analysis procedures. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline across N=500 distinct intents, stratified evenly over 10 synthetic topology profiles (50 intents per profile). Sampling seeds and the deterministic task generator were frozen prior to execution.

Task bank and difficulty taxonomy: Tasks were synthesized by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and encoded the expected_final_state, initial_state, required_sequence, workflow_policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, exactly_active, minimum_active_in_groups) and difficulty metadata (labels such as medium, hard, very_hard and pattern tags: shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change, rolling_access_vlan_migration). Representative tasks (task-000001 … task-000006) and their manifest entries are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl (artifact hash: 5a822e787302a0b3bb03a86a81b20564a44e2636731f853f9d45ac12e4876cc8). Each task manifest entry includes the canonical required_sequence and the constraints enforced by the verifier.

Generation, orchestration, and budget: For each intent the experiment produced a single shared_initial_generation candidate from the declared model gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in execution/model_configuration.json; execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The GVR controller validated the shared candidate with deterministic_netops_validator_v5. If verification failed, at most one automated repair prompt was issued (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Provider audit (deterministic_reconciliation.json) shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 504 with stage_counts mapping shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair = 4, which implements the preregistered maximum_model_calls = 1000 budget and documents low incremental repair cost for this workload.

Deterministic verifier semantics and codebook: The verifier implementation deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performs canonical CLI normalization, syntactic parsing, required‑sequence/workflow policy checks, group/availability constraints, dependency and paired‑field enforcement, and exact final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state. For each episode the verifier emits normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation list, violation_count, and boolean valid. The human‑readable verifier codebook (violation‑code → short description) used both for scoring and for repair prompts is enumerated in the archived execution manifest; the manifest that lists the codebook artifact entry (execution/execution_manifest.json) is included in the evidence bundle for direct retrieval. Representative verifier traces are archived under execution/scoring/ with file examples such as execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json.

Repair policy and prompts: Repairs used a constrained template containing: the original intent abstraction, emitted verifier violation codes and short descriptions, and a request for a corrected canonical CLI sequence. The repair template was intentionally minimal to limit additional model calls and isolate the marginal effect of a single repair attempt. Repair candidates were accepted only if the verifier returned valid=true on the subsequent candidate; repair invocations and acceptance outcomes are logged per episode.

Statistical analysis: The preregistered confirmatory test is the two‑sided conditional exact McNemar on discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01). In the conditional formulation the p‑value is computed as p = 2 * sum_{x=k}^{n} Binom(n, x) * 0.5^{n}, where k = n10 (discordants favouring GVR). The preregistration also declared an exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed by resampling paired outcomes (bootstrap_resamples = 10,000; bootstrap_seed = 1729). Primary missingness rule used complete pairs (complete_pair_primary); the run produced zero failed episodes so no imputation was required.
sections.results:
Execution summary and counts: The run completed completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 intents × 2 conditions) with model_calls_used = 504 and failed_episode_count = 0 (execution manifest timestamps: started_at_utc = 2026-08-29T20:28:23.421646+00:00; completed_at_utc = 2026-08-29T21:33:04.490218+00:00). analysis/condition_summary.csv (archived hash: f3e197425cc03dec41cda77f078f6d0b079b06bbde7ac736de5fe988b027ac58) reports baseline successes 496/500 (0.992) and guarded successes 500/500 (1.000). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; archived hash: 8fb135cec541cbe0b14f16125db33154a41460c49958427fe8e7f3e1f2abfece) is: n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0.

Confirmatory McNemar computation: Observed discordants n = n10 + n01 = 4 with k = n10 = 4. Using the preregistered exact conditional McNemar two‑sided formula, p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5). For n = 4, PBinom(X ≥ 4) = (1/16), so p = 2 * (1/16) = 0.125. Because this exact conditional test was the preregistered decision rule, we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance for the primary estimand.

Exploratory bootstrap interval and interpretation: The preregistered exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729; artifact: analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg) is [0.002, 0.016]. This bootstrap was predeclared exploratory: it resamples paired outcomes without conditioning on observed margins, so it can produce a non‑zero lower bound even when the conditional McNemar p‑value is non‑significant in small‑discordant regimes. With near‑ceiling margins (most pairs concordant) and only four discordants, the bootstrap percentile CI’s frequentist coverage properties are degraded; we therefore report the bootstrap interval descriptively and follow the preregistered conditional McNemar for confirmatory decision making.

Repair diagnostics and representative episode: Repairs were invoked for four initial candidates; each of the four repair prompts produced a subsequent verifier‑passing candidate and corresponds to the four discordant pairs (n10 = 4). Mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 504/500 = 1.008. A representative episode archived at execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json shows shared_initial_candidate and final_configuration equal to:

interface edge1 admin down
interface edge1 mtu 1600
interface edge1 vlan 30
interface edge1 admin up

and verifier_trace entries: difficulty.pattern = shutdown_configure_restore, parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, validator_version = 5.0, valid = true. That JSON file hash is execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json SHA‑256 = e97212b62733ba30de344b8980d06b59cfecb2d791daa91332b3d617a52f45f8 and the shared_initial response artifact is execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt SHA‑256 = f8de4d6e1a625e42ba4907440b4377c78949ed56446e5c73030bc267e56abfaf.

Provider audit and stage accounting: deterministic_reconciliation.json records provider_call_audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 504, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 504, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 504, stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 500, repair = 4. These counts quantify the additional generation cost imposed by the bounded repair policy in this workload.
sections.discussion:
Reconciling inferential perspectives: The GVR pipeline prevented four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that baseline would have accepted. Under the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test this difference is not confirmatory (p = 0.125). The exploratory bootstrap CI excludes zero, but it is explicitly predeclared exploratory and is vulnerable to poor coverage when discordant counts are very small. We therefore present both perspectives, emphasize the preregistered decision rule, and caution readers about overinterpretation of the bootstrap interval in near‑ceiling margins.

What the experiment demonstrates and what it does not: Within the synthetic task bank and the verifier’s rule set, a compact deterministic verifier plus a bounded single‑repair loop intercepted verifier‑detectable hazards at low additional model cost. This supports the proposition that tool‑augmented LLM deployments can reduce verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with modest model overhead. However, passing the deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, validator_version = 5.0) is necessary for the experiment outcome but not sufficient for all production hazards: the verifier does not model vendor‑specific CLI semantics, timing/convergence effects, control‑plane transient hazards, or hardware resource constraints. Operational adoption will require expanded verifier fidelity (vendor parsers, control‑plane simulators) and adversarial NetOps evaluations.

Threats to validity: Internal validity benefits from preregistration, fixed seeds, and complete pairs; no post‑hoc exclusions occurred. Construct validity is limited by synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1 and by verifier abstractions. External validity is constrained by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic tasks; multi‑model replication and real vendor CLI testing are required for generalization. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power plan assumed a larger baseline discordance (target effect ≈ 0.08). The observed near‑ceiling baseline (0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, reducing realized power relative to preregistered assumptions and limiting confirmatory sensitivity. These limitations are documented in the archived manifests and the preregistration.

Operational implications and cost tradeoffs: For settings with verifier‑detectable hazards similar to our synthetic tasks, a bounded repair policy can intercept hazards at low model cost (observed repair rate 4/500). For higher initial hallucination rates or adversarial inputs, repair invocation frequencies and verifier runtimes may materially alter the cost/benefit calculus: the tradeoff involves verifier latency and fidelity vs. the operational risk of unchecked acceptance. Future studies should instrument verifier runtime, multistage repairs, and adversarial robustness.

Reproducibility and artifact grounding: All primary execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle. Key artifact hashes reported inline below allow direct retrieval and verification of the claims and of representative traces used for examples and diagnostics.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 yields an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016], while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in synthetic settings; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated comparator (unexecuted in this run). All primary execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification; representative artifact hashes are provided in the Disclosure Statement below.

The human‑readable verifier codebook (violation‑code → description) is enumerated in the archived execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) and is referenced by repair prompts; the execution manifest in the evidence bundle lists the exact codebook artifact entry and its SHA‑256 for direct retrieval. The design, preregistration, code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and revision were performed autonomously after the autonomy lock; no human manually edited or rewrote manuscript technical content after that lock. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed in this archived run; that unexecuted arm means the originally preregistered two‑test Bonferroni familywise plan could not be fully applied.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan (two confirmatory tests with Bonferroni correction) could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation is partial.
